pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The Resplendent Quetzal Is Easier to Spot in Costa Rica Than Anywhere Else on Earth
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: Costa Rica's cloud forests harbor one of the world's most sought-after birds. The iridescent quetzal feeds on wild avocados in places like Monteverde and Santa Elena — and you don't need a guide to find them if you know when to look. See the full guide to spotting Costa Rica's most iconic bird.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Scarlet Macaws Congregate at Carara National Park Every Morning — Here's Why
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: Carara sits at the intersection of dry forest and humid rainforest, drawing large macaw flocks year-round. Their loud squawks echo before sunrise as dozens of birds gather at traditional roosting trees along the Tarcoles River. See the full guide to macaw watching in Costa Rica.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Tropical Tiger Herons Stand Completely Still for 30 Minutes Before Striking
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: In Costa Rica's rivers and mangrove edges, tiger herons use a sit-and-wait strategy that makes them remarkably easy to observe. Spot one perched on a low branch near water and you might watch it stay frozen for half an hour before snatching a fish in a single dart. See the full guide to Costa Rica's birds.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The Nicoya Peninsula Is One of the World's Official Blue Zones — Here's What That Means
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: Nicoya is one of five confirmed Blue Zones on the planet, where people routinely live past 100 in active, engaged lives. The dry forests, empty beaches, and slow pace are what researchers point to when they explain why locals here outlive the rest of Costa Rica by years. See the full guide to the Nicoya Peninsula.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Tambor's Beaches Have Near-Constant Offshore Breeze — Perfect for Sunset Photography
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The Pacific side of the Nicoya Peninsula catches steady evening winds that flatten the water into a mirror and paint the sky in orange and pink layers. Photographers time their arrivals for about 5:30 pm in the dry season to catch the most consistent light. See the full guide to Tambor and the Nicoya Peninsula.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Howler Monkeys Move Through Tambor's Canopy in Groups of 10 to 30 Every Morning
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The Nicoya Peninsula's howler troupes are among the most vocal in Costa Rica, their deep roars carrying nearly half a kilometer through the trees. A morning walk along the coast road just after sunrise offers the best chance of encountering multiple groups close up. See the full guide to wildlife in the Nicoya Peninsula.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Costa Rica's Waterfalls Are Tallest in the Central Valley — Within an Hour of San José
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The waterfall circuit near San José — including Zurquí, Cascade, and the waterfalls around Heredia — drops through cloud forest with vertical drops that rival anything in the Americas. The green moss, mist, and ferns make the surrounding jungle as compelling as the falls themselves. See the full guide to Costa Rica's waterfalls.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The Falls Near La Paz Have Sloth Families That Pose Better Than the Waterfalls
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The La Paz Waterfall Gardens area shelters multiple sloth territories along the walking trails, with mothers and juveniles regularly spotted in the Cecropia trees just meters from the main viewing platforms. Combine waterfall viewing with sloth photography without leaving the same property. See the full guide to Costa Rica's waterfalls.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Nobody Hikes the Full Waterfall Trail in Guanacaste in Dry Season — That's the Best Time
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The waterfall circuit in Guanacaste is at its most dramatic between December and April, when reduced water flow creates cleaner cascades and the surrounding forest stays a vivid deep green. Fewer hikers mean you can photograph the falls without anyone in the frame. See the full guide to Guanacaste's waterfalls.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Costa Rica Produces More Scenic Aerial Photography Per Square Kilometer Than Most Countries
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The combination of volcanic peaks, coastal cliffs, cloud forest canopy, and river valleys creates visual density that few destinations can match. Aerial shots from drones over Arenal, the Gulf of Nicoya, and the Osa Peninsula consistently outperform static landscape images in engagement. See the full guide to Costa Rica photography.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The Dry Season Landscape in Guanacaste Looks Like a Nature Documentary in Person
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: Between January and April, Guanacaste's deciduous trees drop their leaves and the hills turn golden, creating sweeping vistas that look post-processed but are completely natural. The contrast between green river valleys and golden hillsides makes this one of the most photographed landscapes in Central America. See the full guide to Guanacaste.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The San José Skyline Looks Best at Golden Hour From the Hills Above Escazú
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: Escazú hills offer a rare elevated perspective over Costa Rica's capital, with the city grid framed by mountain silhouettes at sunrise and sunset. Morning fog often settles below the viewpoint level, creating layered panoramic scenes that most visitors never see. See the full guide to photographing San José.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: Jaco Beach Is the Closest Surf Town to San José — Two Hours Door to Beach
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: Jacó sits roughly 100 kilometers from San José, making it the most accessible Pacific beach break in Costa Rica. Consistent offshore winds keep the water clean most mornings, and the town has enough infrastructure that you can arrive with just a board and find everything else you need. See the full guide to Jacó Beach.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The Sunset From Jaco's Beachfront Is a Daily Event — Tourists and Locals Alike Stop to Watch
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: The Pacific coast orientation means Jacó faces almost due west, placing the sunset directly over open ocean without obstruction. During the dry season months of December through March, the sky tends toward vivid orange and purple layers that photographers can capture without special equipment. See the full guide to Jacó Beach.

pinterest_entries_in_queue.title: The Highland Ridge Above Jaco Catches Cloud Formations That Roll in From the Pacific
pinterest_entries_in_queue.description: On most mornings between June and November, low-altitude clouds drift through the hills behind Jacó, creating atmospheric layers that are especially dramatic in wide landscape shots. The transition from clear coast to misty ridge happens within an hour of sunrise and lasts until mid-morning. See the full guide to photographing Jacó's surrounding landscape.
